Unit 02 · Chapter 1

Feed-Forward Networks

CSE 30124 · Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
William Theisen · University of Notre Dame
Feed-Forward Networks01

Linear Decision Boundaries

In Model Evaluation we asked "Did we win?" and a logistic regression answered with a straight line through the two teams' yards, getting 83.7% of unseen games right. Let's ask a different question about the same games: "Was it close?" Call a game a one-score game if it was decided by 8 points or fewer (a touchdown and a two-point conversion), which 55 of our 141 games were.

The close games sit in a strip along the diagonal, with blowouts on both sides. Logistic regression gets only 67.4% of the games right, and it isn't the fit's fault. The best any straight line can do is 88.7%, by cutting off one side of the strip and leaving the other side's blowouts in with the close games. It's the XOR problem again, this time with our data.

(Asking this of the final score is a little silly, since we could just subtract. It's here for the shape.)

Feed-Forward Networks · From Lines to Networks02

Multi-Layer Perceptrons

In the Perceptron chapter no single perceptron could solve XOR, but two side by side (an OR and a NAND) followed by a third (an AND) could. The same trick works here. One line asks "did Notre Dame win by more than 8?", another asks "did Notre Dame lose by more than 8?", and a game is close when both answers are no.

Stacking perceptrons like this, so some take the outputs of others as their inputs, gives a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). Frank Rosenblatt described networks like this in the 1960s, though in his only the last layer could learn and the earlier ones were fixed, a problem we'll come back to at the end of the chapter.

Feed-Forward Networks · From Lines to Networks03

The Artificial Neuron

A perceptron's step function only ever says yes or no. Logistic Regression gave us a softer version, the sigmoid, which also says how sure it is. A perceptron with a smooth activation like this is usually called an artificial neuron (a loose nod to biology, where a neuron fires once its input passes a threshold).

It takes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, z = ω1x1 + ω2x2 + b, called the pre-activation, then passes z through an activation function (here the sigmoid, σ) to get its output. The weights and bias are its learnable parameters.

Feed-Forward Networks · From Lines to Networks04

One Neuron, One Line

The numbers in that figure are a "won by more than 8?" neuron on a 10-point win. Drawn over every possible score, the neuron is a line with a soft edge, h near 0 on one side of z = 0 and near 1 on the other:

A 9-point win would only get 0.73, soft for a hard cutoff, so our network multiplies the weights by 10 and sets the bias to −85. The switch then sits at 8.5, and every real score lands within 0.007 of 0 or 1.

Feed-Forward Networks · From Lines to Networks05

Feed-Forward Networks

Three of these neurons, arranged like our MLP, make a feed-forward neural network (FFN). Each column of neurons is a layer.

The input layer is just the feature vector, the two teams' points, and has no neurons. The hidden layer holds h1 and h2, called hidden because their values never appear in the data, we only ever see the inputs and the label. The output layer holds ŷ, the network's answer. Data only flows forward, with no loops, hence the name.

A layer where every neuron takes every output of the layer before is a fully connected layer (also called a dense or linear layer). The number of layers is a network's depth and the number of neurons in a layer its width, and deep learning is the study of networks with many layers. Ours, with 9 learnable parameters, is about as shallow as they come.

Feed-Forward Networks · Feed-Forward Networks06

The Forward Pass

Here are the weights for our network:

h_1 = \sigma(\wnum{10}x_1 - \wnum{10}x_2 - \bnum{85}) \qquad h_2 = \sigma(\wnum{10}x_2 - \wnum{10}x_1 - \bnum{85}) \yhat = \sigma(\bnum{2} - \wnum{4} h_1 - \wnum{4} h_2)

Read neuron by neuron, h1 is 1 when Notre Dame won by more than 8 and 0 otherwise, and h2 is the same for losses. The output starts at σ(2) = 0.88 and drops to σ(−2) = 0.12 when either hidden neuron fires, so the output neuron says "neither", which is exactly a one-score game.

Computing the output from the inputs like this is called the forward pass. Here it is on four games, calling a game close when ŷ is above 0.5:

gamescoreh1h2ŷclose?
2014 North Carolina50–43000.88yes
2015 Clemson22–24000.88yes
2012 Wake Forest38–0100.12no
2012 Alabama (title game)14–42010.12no
Feed-Forward Networks · Feed-Forward Networks07

Decision Regions

Each hidden neuron switches on past its own line, so over every possible score the output says "close" only between the two lines. The parts of the plane where a network gives each answer are its decision regions, and ours is a strip:

On all 141 games it gets every one right (100%), where no straight line can do better than 88.7%. There's nothing here to overfit, the rule is exact, so it would do just as well on games it has never seen.

Feed-Forward Networks · Feed-Forward Networks08

Hidden Features

So why can three neurons do what no line could? Look at what the hidden layer hands on. Every game comes out of it as a pair of numbers, (h1, h2), and since each is within 0.007 of 0 or 1, every game lands on a corner:

On the right the close games sit in a strip no line can cut out. After the hidden layer, on the left, the same 55 games all sit at (0, 0), the 70 big wins at (1, 0) and the 16 big losses at (0, 1), and the output neuron's line, h1 + h2 = 0.5, separates them perfectly. The output neuron is just a logistic regression, the hidden layer moved the games somewhere a line works.

This is the real power of a hidden layer. In Linear Regression we added features like x2 by hand and had to guess which would help. A hidden layer computes its own features from the inputs (here "won big" and "lost big"), and the next layer only has to draw a line through them.

Feed-Forward Networks · Why Networks Work09

Non-Linearity

Does the hidden layer need its sigmoids to build those features? Let's take them out and see. Without them h1 + h2 = −170 for every game, since the 10x1 and 10x2 terms cancel and the two biases add up. The output neuron's pre-activation is then 682 whatever the score was, and the network calls all 141 games close (39.0% right). The two neurons cancel out.

Here is every game at the output neuron's pre-activation, which says "close" right of the dashed line. With the sigmoids the close games and the rest land on opposite sides, without them all 141 land in the same spot:

Feed-Forward Networks · Why Networks Work10

Linear Layers Collapse

That isn't bad luck with our weights. A layer with no activation function is a linear transformation of its inputs (a weighted sum plus a bias, as in Linear Regression), and a linear transformation of a linear transformation is still linear:

\bp{X \Omega_1\T + b_1} \Omega_2\T + b_2 = X \bp{\Omega_2 \Omega_1}\T + \bp{b_1 \Omega_2\T + b_2}

However many layers we stack, without activation functions they collapse into a single layer with weights ω2 ω1, which can only draw the one straight line a logistic regression could. (Ours collapses to ω2 ω1 = [0, 0], no line at all.)

So the activation function's real job is to introduce non-linearity. Without the bend, the "new features" are just the old ones stretched and rotated, and a line through them is still a line through the original points.

Feed-Forward Networks · Why Networks Work11

More Neurons, More Shapes

Each hidden neuron draws one line, so more neurons means more lines to build a shape from. Take a narrower question: was it a shootout, a one-score game where both teams scored 28 or more (four touchdowns)? 18 of our 141 games were.

Two more hidden neurons, h3 = σ(275 − 10x1) for "Notre Dame scored under 28" and h4 = σ(275 − 10x2) for the opponent, cap the strip. The output neuron is the same idea as before, σ(2 − 4h1 − 4h2 − 4h3 − 4h4). It says yes only when none of the four fire, and it gets all 141 games right.

Every hidden neuron adds an edge, and an output neuron that wants all of them quiet (an AND) carves out the region they surround. One that fires when any of them does (an OR) would glue regions together instead.

Feed-Forward Networks · Why Networks Work12

Universal Approximation

How far does this go? The universal approximation theorem says a network with a single hidden layer, given enough hidden neurons, can approximate any continuous function as closely as we like (Cybenko proved it for sigmoids in 1989, Hornik for almost any activation in 1991).

A steep sigmoid is nearly a step, one step per neuron. Here are Notre Dame's points per game each season, fit by networks and by two models we've met before:

All three get there given enough capacity. A fine enough staircase can follow any smooth curve (or, with two inputs, any shape we could draw).

Unfortunately the theorem only says the right weights exist, not how many neurons it takes or how to find them. In practice several smaller layers do far more than one enormous one, the "deep" in deep learning.

Feed-Forward Networks · Why Networks Work13

Layers as Matrices

Networks with that many neurons need a compact way to be written down. Much like we stacked our games into a matrix X in Linear Regression, we can stack a layer's neurons into a weight matrix ω, one row per neuron and one column per input, with their biases in a row b. A whole layer, for every game at once, is then one matrix multiplication:

Z = X \Omega\T + b \qquad A = \sigma(Z)

Pictured above is our whole network this way, with all 141 games in X. ω1 is 2 × 2 (two neurons, two inputs), so X ω1T is 141 × 2, a row per game and a column per hidden neuron. The output layer has one neuron with two inputs, so ω2 is 1 × 2 and its transpose 2 × 1, which turns the hidden layer's 141 × 2 into 141 × 1, one ŷ per game. Getting the shapes to line up is most of the work of writing a network down.

Feed-Forward Networks · Why Networks Work14

Activation Functions

Any non-linear function will do as the bend, the universal approximation theorem only needs one. Three are common, the sigmoid, the hyperbolic tangent (tanh) and the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU):

\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}} \gold{\tanh}(z) = \frac{e^{z} - e^{-z}}{e^{z} + e^{-z}} = 2\,\sigma(2z) - 1 \gold{\mathrm{relu}}(z) = \max(0, z)

The sigmoid is still the usual activation on the output of a binary classifier, since its output reads as a probability. Tanh is a sigmoid stretched to run from −1 to 1, centered on 0, long the standard for hidden layers. Both are soft steps, which is why stacking them made a staircase on the last few pages. ReLU is a different shape altogether, 0 and then a straight ramp.

Feed-Forward Networks · Activation Functions15

ReLU

ReLU builds with ramps instead of steps. Here are the same seasons with 10 ReLU neurons, one bend at each season, where each neuron's weight is how much the slope changes there:

The result is the seasons joined by straight lines, a curve made of straight pieces, and with enough pieces that can be any curve. In Linear Regression a single straight line was all we had, here a network glues together as many as it needs. ReLU is also cheap (one comparison, no exponential) and, for reasons we'll see when we train networks, the most common activation in modern neural networks.

Our close-game network works with ReLUs too. h1 = relu(x1 − x2 − 8) is how many points past 8 Notre Dame won by (and 0 otherwise), h2 = relu(x2 − x1 − 8) is the same for losses, and with the same output neuron, σ(2 − 4h1 − 4h2), it still gets all 141 games right. Notice that it needs no steepness factor, since any blowout makes h1 or h2 at least 1.

Feed-Forward Networks · Activation Functions16

Multi-Class Classification

The output neuron only ever sees the hidden features, and nothing stops several output neurons from reading the same ones. That lets one network answer a question with more than two answers. What if we wanted to know whether Notre Dame won by more than 8, the game was within one score, or Notre Dame lost by more than 8? With our 8-point cut that's 70, 55 and 16 games.

A task with more than two possible labels is a multi-class classification task. Our output neuron can only answer one yes-or-no question, so we give the output layer one neuron per outcome:

The hidden layer is the same as before. Each output neuron scores one outcome, z1 = 2h1 for a win by more than 8, z2 = 2 − 2h1 − 2h2 for a one-score game and z3 = 2h2 for a loss by more than 8. Whichever outcome actually happened gets a score of 2 and the other two get 0.

Feed-Forward Networks · Activation Functions17

Softmax

Scores aren't probabilities. A sigmoid on each output neuron would give three numbers between 0 and 1, but nothing would make them add up to 1. Instead we use softmax, which exponentiates every score and divides by the total:

\text{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{K} e^{z_j}}

For 2014 North Carolina (50 to 43), z = [0, 2, 0] and softmax gives 0.11, 0.79 and 0.11, mostly a close game. For 2021 North Carolina (44 to 34), z = [2, 0, 0] gives 0.79 for a Notre Dame win by more than 8. Taking the biggest probability as the answer, the network gets all 141 games right.

The biggest score always gets the biggest probability, so softmax is the usual last-layer activation of a classifier. With two outcomes it's exactly the sigmoid of the difference between the two scores, which is why we never needed it before. Training a network like this needs a loss for more than two outcomes (categorical cross-entropy), which comes in the next chapter.

Feed-Forward Networks · Activation Functions18

Computation Graphs

To measure how well a network does we wrap a loss around its output, for our close-game question the binary cross-entropy from Logistic Regression (0.13 on all 141 games). Each step of the forward pass, from X to the loss, uses the results of earlier steps. Drawing every step as a node and every dependency as an arrow gives the network's computation graph:

The forward pass computes each node from its parents, top to bottom. Since each node's output is the next node's input, the whole graph can also be written as one statement of nested functions:

L = \text{BCE}\bp{\sigma\bp{\sigma\bp{X \Omega_1\T + b_1} \Omega_2\T + b_2},\ y}
Feed-Forward Networks · Activation Functions19

Tensors

Three games by hand is fine, all 141 is tedious, and real networks have millions of weights. From here on we'll build networks with PyTorch, a Python library for neural networks first built at Facebook (now Meta). Its version of a numpy array is the tensor, and arithmetic works just as it does in numpy, @ for matrix multiplication and .T for the transpose. Here's our hidden layer on three games (in code we write W1 for ω1, since ω is hard to type):

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
import torch
X = torch.tensor([[50., 43.], [38., 0.], [14., 42.]])
W1 = torch.tensor([[10., -10.], [-10., 10.]])
b1 = torch.tensor([-85., -85.])
A1 = torch.sigmoid(X @ W1.T + b1) # b1 is added to every row
print(X.shape, W1.shape, b1.shape)
print(A1.round(decimals=3))
Output
torch.Size([3, 2]) torch.Size([2, 2]) torch.Size([2])
tensor([[0., 0.],
        [1., 0.],
        [0., 1.]])

X @ W1.T has shape [3, 2] and b1 only [2], so PyTorch adds b1 to every row. Stretching the smaller tensor to fit like this is called broadcasting, and it means the same line works for any number of games. Unlike a numpy array, a tensor can live on a GPU, which is where real networks are trained.

Feed-Forward Networks · PyTorch20

Layers and Activations in PyTorch

We rarely write out X @ W1.T + b1 ourselves. PyTorch has the fully connected layer pre-built as nn.Linear, and nn.Linear(2, 2) is a layer with 2 inputs and 2 neurons. Its .weight is our ω1, stored one row per neuron as we've been writing it, and its .bias is our b1. The activation functions are built in too:

1

4

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
torch.set_printoptions(precision=2)
fc1 = nn.Linear(2, 2) # 2 inputs, 2 neurons
print(fc1.weight.shape, fc1.bias.shape)
print(torch.relu(torch.tensor([-3., 0., 5.])))
z = torch.tensor([[0., 2., 0.], [2., 0., 0.]])
print(torch.softmax(z, dim=1)) # one row per game
Output
torch.Size([2, 2]) torch.Size([2])
tensor([0., 0., 5.])
tensor([[0.11, 0.79, 0.11],
        [0.79, 0.11, 0.11]])

The two rows of z are our softmax examples, 2014 and 2021 North Carolina, and we get back the same 0.11, 0.79 and 0.11. dim=1 tells softmax that each game's scores run along a row, so each row adds up to 1, not each column.

Feed-Forward Networks · PyTorch21

Neural Networks in PyTorch

A whole network is a class with its layers in __init__ and its forward pass in forward. Here's ours, run on all 141 games. Normally training sets the weights, so copying ours in under torch.no_grad() is a trick for this chapter only:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import pandas as pd
class CloseGame(nn.Module):
def __init__(self):
super().__init__()
self.fc1 = nn.Linear(2, 2)
self.fc2 = nn.Linear(2, 1)
def forward(self, x):
a_1 = torch.sigmoid(self.fc1(x))
return torch.sigmoid(self.fc2(a_1))
model = CloseGame()
with torch.no_grad(): # our hand-picked weights
model.fc1.weight[:] = torch.tensor([[10., -10.],
[-10., 10.]])
model.fc1.bias[:] = torch.tensor([-85., -85.])
model.fc2.weight[:] = torch.tensor([[-4., -4.]])
model.fc2.bias[:] = torch.tensor([2.])
games = pd.read_csv("nd_football.csv")
pts = games[["nd_points", "opponent_points"]].values
X = torch.tensor(pts, dtype=torch.float32)
close = (X[:, 0] - X[:, 1]).abs() <= 8
y_hat = model(X)[:, 0]
right = ((y_hat > 0.5) == close).sum().item()
print(right, "of", len(X))
Output
141 of 141
Feed-Forward Networks · PyTorch22

Training a Neural Network

Our network gets every game right only because we set its weights by hand, which gets us no further than Rosenblatt. What we need is the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight, so gradient descent can adjust them all at once. As a model runs, PyTorch records every operation in a computation graph:

The algorithm that walks this graph backwards, from the loss up to every weight, is backpropagation, made the standard way to train networks by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams in 1986 (the idea goes back to Linnainmaa in 1970). It's the subject of the next chapter.
